newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metalworkers near deal in last major region.
newsitem.headline: German metalworkers near deal in last major region.

text.p: German metal and engineering workers in the southern region of Nordwuerttemberg went into pay talks with employers on Tuesday confident they could a force a climb-down on planned cuts to labour costs.
Much of the cost-cutting was orginally due to come from a new law introduced in October which allowed employers to reduce sick pay from its current 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.

But following mass protests and the threat of strikes by workers in the already hard-hit industry, most of Germany's metal and engineering firms have now backed away from introducing the law into new worker contracts.

Going into the negotiations held in the town of Stuttgart, regional employers' negotiator Klaus Fritsche acknowledged that there was little scope for employers to seek a more favourable wage pact in the Nordwuerttemberg region.
"We are realistic enough to see that," he told journalists. Union officials had earlier said they were confident that a deal securing full sick pay could be agreed.
Nordwuerttemberg, where some 600,000 workers are employed in the sector, is the last big engineering region where accords guaranteeing workers continued sick pay at full salary have not been signed.

Following a break-through deal signed in the northern state of Lower Saxony two weeks ago, contracts securing full sick pay have now been signed for some two-thirds of the 3.2 million workers in the west German metal and engineering sectors.

The Lower Saxony agreement, which has been adopted by regions including the steel-producing state of North Rhine-Westphalia and the large Bavarian engineering region, includes a 1.5 pay rise next year and 2.5 percent in 1998.

Including small reductions in worker bonuses that employers were able to secure, the accords are calculated to increase labour costs in the industry by less than one percent next year, and by slightly more in 1998.

While significantly lower than the wage deal agreed for 1996, it means that employers will once again have failed to bring in the deep reduction in labour costs they have for years been crying out for.
Some 180,000 engineering workers in the northern German coastal region have yet to reach a wage deal with employers.
